newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH, UKRAINIAN LEADERS PLAN EVER CLOSER LINKS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH, UKRAINIAN LEADERS PLAN EVER CLOSER LINKS.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma of Ukraine and Aleksander Kwasniewski of Poland on Thursday outlined plans to step up political and economic exchanges this year to cement warm ties both see as crucial to their region.

During a one-day working visit by Kuchma to Warsaw they oversaw the signing of a memorandum, like one Poland clinched with Russia last year, on their desire to liberalise trade and create a mutual free trade zone at some time in the future.

Kuchma was invited by the Polish Business Club employers group to receive a man of the year award for market reforms that have boosted bilateral trade and he grabbed the chance for talks with Kwasniewski, alone and then with advisers.

Poland, well on course for its top goals of joining the European Union and NATO, restated it would be a tireless advocate for its larger ex-Soviet neighbour's efforts to bind itself to Central and Western European groupings.

Kwasniewski vowed to back Ukraine's aim of clinching an association agreement with the EU and joining the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), and offered Polish experts' advice for Ukraine's economic reforms.

He said the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation should reach a special charter with Ukraine, like that which the Western pact is discussing with Russia -- a country that, unlike Ukraine, opposes NATO's enlargement to embrace Poland.

"I think an enlarged NATO should have an appropriate, separate treaty with Ukraine, because without Ukraine it is hard to imagine a system of common European security," he told a news conference after the talks.
"I thank you very much for your understanding and support," said Kuchma.

The presidents set out proposals to boost growing economic ties, which Kuchma said would be carried further by Polish business representatives in Kiev this month and a March visit to Warsaw by Ukraine's Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko.

Poland's bilateral trade with Ukraine exceeded $1 billion for the first time in 1995 and from January to September last year totalled $1.4 billion -- a rise of 39 percent over the same period 1995, according to Polish economy ministry figures.

The data, quoted by PAP news agency, showed the balance of trade firmly in Poland's favour, with exports totalling $1 billion in the first nine months of 1996 and consisting of chemicals, coal, food products and electronics.

Poland, which imports mainly iron ore, chemicals and grain from Ukraine, also has investments in some 400 firms there and Kuchma said a tax reform he planned for the first quarter would encourage further investment by Poland's fast-growing economy.

Polish-Ukrainian relations have historically been troubled and both countries are drafting a declaration of reconciliation on painful issues -- including a grim revolt by Ukrainians in east Poland after World War Two which Warsaw's then-communist authorities ended by a harsh mass deportation.
Kwasniewski said he was sure the historic document, settling the past to prepare for a positive future, would be ready for adoption when he visited Kiev officially in May.

Both presidents, who with Lithuania's Algirdas Brazauskas voiced concern for democracy in Belarus as President Alexander Lukashenko clashed with parliament last year, said it was important to keep talking to Minsk and not to isolate it.
"If Poland and Ukraine turn their backs on Belarus, Belarus will have a road open only to Moscow," Kwasniewski said.
Both said they did not oppose some closer Belarussian economic and political integration with Russia but backed the existence of a sovereign Belarus.
